rationale: Chutkan's documentation of Western microbial diversity loss provides a concrete empirical example of the 'environmental and microbial associations' in Yamada's multistage IBD model — the depletion of microbial diversity is one specific environmental perturbation that converges with genetic susceptibility to drive IBD.

Yamada's multistage IBD model demonstrates that at least one autoimmune-type disease (IBD) arises from a gut-centered interaction of genetics, microbes, and environment — providing specific mechanistic evidence that supports Campbell-McBride's broader claim that all autoimmunity is born in the gut, though it does not prove the claim for non-gut autoimmune diseases.

Chutkan's dysbiosis concept provides the specific vocabulary for the 'microbial associations' component of Yamada's multistage IBD model — dysbiosis (diminution of beneficial bacteria, flourishing of pathogens) is the microbial state that interacts with genetic susceptibility and environmental triggers in IBD pathogenesis.

Chutkan's leaky gut model provides the mechanistic interface between the 'microbial associations' and the immune dysregulation in Yamada's multistage model — increased intestinal permeability is the pathway by which dysbiotic microbial products cross the epithelial barrier and trigger the immune response that drives IBD.

Gottschall's vicious cycle provides a specific, mechanistically detailed example of how an environmental factor (carbohydrate malabsorption) drives a self-reinforcing cycle of microbial fermentation, mucosal injury, and further malabsorption — a concrete instance of the environmental-microbial interaction that Yamada's multistage model posits.

Yamada's multistage model contextualizes and refines Foote's simplified claim that CD is caused by an 'overactive immune system' — showing that immune dysregulation is not a standalone cause but one component interacting with genetic predisposition, microbial composition, and environmental triggers.

The elemental diet's mechanism of starving colonic bacteria of substrate provides therapeutic evidence for the microbial component of Yamada's multistage IBD model — reducing bacterial load through dietary substrate deprivation improves IBD outcomes, confirming that microbes play a causal role in disease activity.

The GAPS Introduction Diet's three mechanisms (nourishing the gut lining, removing fiber irritants, delivering probiotic microbes) provide a therapeutic framework that simultaneously addresses the environmental and microbial components of Yamada's multistage IBD model — demonstrating a practical protocol targeting multiple stages of the disease process.

Campbell-McBride's clinical recommendation that IBD patients require the Introduction Diet provides clinical-practice support for Yamada's multistage model — the therapeutic targeting of environmental and microbial factors (dietary modification) in IBD patients validates the model's assertion that these factors are causally important.

Sonnenburg's 'second genome' concept elaborates the microbial component of Yamada's multistage IBD model at a systems level — the 2+ million microbial genes represent a malleable environmental-genetic interface whose depletion through Western lifestyle explains why the microbial contribution to IBD varies across populations.

Myers' quantification of genetic vs environmental contribution (25%/75%) directly supports and extends Yamada's multistage IBD model by providing rough weighting to the relative contributions — the predominance of environmental factors aligns with the model's emphasis on microbial and environmental associations beyond genetics alone.

The UC diagnostic requirement for endoscopy and histology explains one driver of the 4-6 year IBS diagnostic delay — ruling out IBD (UC/CD) requires costly, invasive procedures (colonoscopy with biopsy), and patients cycle through these before receiving an IBS diagnosis by exclusion.
